title: Implement Disaster Recovery Processes
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 7: Security Operations: Implement Disaster Recovery Processes.

items: DRP — plan for recovering IT systems and operations after a disaster
BCP focuses on keeping the business running during a disaster; DRP focuses on restoring IT after a disaster
DRP is a subset of the broader BCP program
Key components: recovery procedures, roles and responsibilities, communication plans, testing schedules
Disaster assessment — initial evaluation to determine the extent of damage and required recovery actions
May require transferring operations to an alternative facility

rows: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time
How much data can you afford to lose?
Maximum time to restore system functionality
Time to verify system integrity, test, and make ready for production
Time between system restoration and full operation
Maximum Tolerable Downtime / Maximum Allowable Downtime
Maximum total time a process can be disrupted before unacceptable impact

items: Relationship: RTO + WRT ≤ MTD
RPO drives backup frequency — if RPO = 4 hours, backups must occur at least every 4 hours
RTO drives recovery site selection — lower RTO requires more ready sites (hot > warm > cold)
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) — average time a system operates before failure; higher = more reliable
MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) — average time to repair a failed system; lower = faster recovery

blocks.text: Understanding the relationships between these metrics is essential:

items: MTD/MAD is the overarching constraint — the absolute maximum time a business process can be down before causing unacceptable damage. This is determined by the Business Impact Analysis (BIA).
RTO is the target for restoring system functionality — must be less than MTD.
WRT is the time needed after system restoration to verify integrity, test functionality, and return to full production. RTO + WRT must not exceed MTD.
RPO is independent of the downtime metrics — it measures acceptable data loss. An RPO of zero means no data loss is acceptable (requiring synchronous replication).

blocks.text: How to reduce the cost of BCP and DRP plans: "The more quickly a given process needs to be recovered, the more expensive it is going to be" (Destination CISSP). Organizations must balance recovery objectives against budget:

items: RPO near zero → expensive real-time replication
RTO near zero → expensive hot/mirrored sites
Longer RPO/RTO → cheaper backup/recovery options

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: RTO + WRT ≤ MTD. If the question asks about the MAXIMUM time a business function can be down, the answer is MTD, not RTO. RTO is when the system is restored; WRT is the additional time to verify and test. Together they must not exceed MTD.

rows: Review plan on paper; individuals verify their responsibilities
Team walks through the plan together in a meeting; discuss each step
Simulate a disaster scenario; team practices response procedures (no actual systems affected)
Activate recovery systems alongside production; production continues normally
Shut down production and activate recovery systems; most realistic but highest risk

items: Start with less disruptive tests and progress to more realistic ones as confidence grows
DRP tests should be conducted at least annually and after significant changes to the environment
Document test results and update the plan based on lessons learned

blocks.text: DR testing is essential because an untested plan is unreliable. Organizations should begin with lower-risk tests (checklist, walkthrough) and progress to more realistic tests (parallel, full interruption) as the plan matures and confidence grows. The full interruption test is the most realistic and provides the highest confidence that the plan will work in an actual disaster. However, it also carries the highest risk because production operations are actually shut down. A full interruption test failure could result in an actual unplanned outage. The parallel test is often the best compromise — it activates recovery systems and processes real data alongside production, providing high confidence without risking production operations. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Full interruption test = most realistic but highest risk. Parallel test = activates DR systems while production continues. The exam often asks which test type provides the most confidence with acceptable risk — parallel test is usually the answer in business-focused scenarios.

items: A disaster has different aspects: natural disasters (earthquake, flood, hurricane), man-made disasters (fire, explosion, cyberattack), and utility failures (power, water, communications)
Emergency response — immediate actions to protect life safety and minimize damage
Crisis communications — pre-established communication plans for notifying employees, customers, partners, and media
Succession planning — identifying who takes over critical roles if key personnel are unavailable

Duress codes — covert signals to indicate that an employee is acting under coercion; should be changed regularly and include training for particularly vulnerable employees (senior executives, employees in high-risk areas)
